**The government gave this aeroplane an X number in 2021 and then spent twenty-nine million dollars on it without once writing the number down.**

The federal award record carries 73 transactions against this aircraft, running from 21 February 2014 to 30 September 2025 and totalling 29,085,924.37 dollars \[[USAspending][ref_usaspending]\]. **Not one of them calls it the X-62A.** They call it VISTA, or the variable stability in-flight simulator, or the airframe. The designation was allocated on 14 June 2021 \[[DOD 4120.15-L Addendum][ref_mds_addendum]\], and by the date of this article, 1,637 days later, the accounting system that pays for the aeroplane has still never used it.

**That is not an argument that the designation is unimportant. It is a measurement of where a designation lives.** The register records it, the press releases use it, the school that flies the aeroplane is proud of it, and the contracting officers who buy its maintenance have no use for it at all.

This is the sixty-third article in the [X-Planes series][related_post_a297_framing], following the [X-1][related_post_a298_bell_x1], the [X-2][related_post_a299_bell_x2], the The [previous article][related_post_a358_dynetics_x61_gremlins] established that the register stops being a primary source at the X-61A, because the compiler's note says that for allocations after October 2018 the official description is no longer releasable to the public and prints the reconstructed ones in blue \[[DOD 4120.15-L Addendum][ref_mds_addendum]\]. **This is the second article on the far side of that line and the finding holds.** Of the 31 rows whose designation begins with the letter X, 22 carry official wording and 9 do not, and this is one of the 9.

The reconstruction reads as follows.

> *VISTA*; NF-16D redesignated after upgrade for "Skyborg" program

That is 62 characters including the popular name and 55 without it, against a median of 110 across the X rows and 99 across the whole register. **Only 2 of the 31 X rows carry a shorter one.**

### One Word in This Row Appears Nowhere Else in the Register

**The word `redesignated` appears in exactly 1 row of all 539, and this is it.** That was measured against the parsed register rather than remembered.

The idea is not unique. 8 of the 31 X rows describe an aircraft modified from an existing one. **What is unique is the verb.** The other 7 say *highly modified*, or *converted*, or *derivative of*, or *upgrade*. **Only this one says the aeroplane was renamed**, which is a statement about paperwork rather than about metal, and it is the only row in the register that makes one.

**That is fitting, because renaming is the closest thing to a modification this particular allocation involved.** The aeroplane had been flying for 29.2 years when it became an X-plane. It was not built for the number, it was not rebuilt for the number, and the number did not change what it does.

## The Research Question

**The aeroplane is not the subject and an article that treated it as one would have nothing to say.**

The X-62A is a two-seat F-16D. Its span is the F-16's span, its wing area is the F-16's wing area, its engine is a production fighter engine, and its performance is tabulated in every reference work that covers the type \[[General Dynamics F-16 Fighting Falcon][ref_f16]\]. Nothing about the airframe is a research question and nothing in this article will pretend otherwise.

**What is a research question is whether one aeroplane can be made to behave like a different aeroplane, closely enough that the pilot flying the first cannot tell it from the second.** That is a control problem, it has an exact statement, and it has an exact condition for solvability that was written down in a NASA Technical Memorandum dated 18 October 1967, twenty-four years before this aeroplane first flew \[[Erzberger, Analysis and Design of Model Following Control Systems by State Space Techniques, NASA Technical Memorandum X-61189, 18 October 1967][ref_erzberger_1967]\]. **The condition is a statement about the host aeroplane's controls and not about its performance**, which is why the vehicle drops out of the argument almost immediately and why this article spends its arithmetic on a matrix rather than on a flight envelope.

The sections below establish four things. **The condition for exact model following is a subspace containment**, and it says how many independent controls an in-flight simulator needs and in which axes. **The determinant that decides whether those controls are independent is a distance**, being the separation between two surfaces measured in chords. **The frequency at which the simulation runs out of authority is published**, in a table of deflection and rate limits that NASA released in 1979, and for one surface it falls below a fighter's own short period. And **an in-flight simulator cannot reproduce an aeroplane quicker than its own hardware**, which makes the set of aeroplanes it can imitate one-sided in a way no amount of software will fix.

**The economics and the paperwork are treated as records in their own right** rather than as background, because the contract record for this aeroplane answers a question that neither of the previous two articles could ask. The X-60A's money and the X-61A's money paid for a development programme with a beginning and an end. **This money pays to keep one aeroplane flying**, in calendar-year increments, for a decade, and it therefore measures what an instrument of this kind costs to own.

## The Name Does Not Spell Its Own Acronym

**VISTA has been expanded 7 different ways in the federal award record for this one aeroplane**, across 55 occurrences. That is a count of the government's own descriptions of its own contracts.

| Expansion | Occurrences | Keeps the word stability |
|---|---|---|
| Variable stability in-flight simulator and test aircraft | 23 | yes |
| Variable stability in-flight simulator | 21 | yes |
| Variable stability in-flight simulator test aircraft | 5 | yes |
| Variable in-flight stability test aircraft | 2 | yes |
| Variable stability inflight simulator test aircraft | 2 | yes |
| Variable in-flight simulator test aircraft | 1 | no |
| Variable stability in-flight test aircraft | 1 | yes |

**54 of the 55 keep the word `stability` and 1 drops it.** The contracting system is consistent about the one word and inconsistent about everything else, including whether the aeroplane is a simulator, a test aircraft, or both, and including where the hyphen goes.

**Now count the letters.** Variable, stability, in-flight, simulator, test, aircraft gives V, S, I, S, T, A. **The acronym is VISTA and the expansion spells VSISTA.** The word `stability`, which the award record preserves in 54 of 55 descriptions, contributes no letter at all. **It has always been a silent S.**

**And the aeroplane's prime contractor has now fixed it.** Lockheed Martin's announcement of the artificial-intelligence flights writes the name as **Variable In-flight Simulation Test Aircraft** \[[VISTA X-62 Advancing Autonomy and Changing the Face of Air Power, Lockheed Martin, 13 February 2023][ref_lm_press]\], which does spell VISTA, letter for letter, with nothing left over. **The repair was made by deleting the word that never fitted.**

**The consequence is not cosmetic.** The original name says the aeroplane's variable quantity is its stability. The corrected name says the variable quantity is the simulation. **Those are different claims about what the machine is for**, and the second is the better description of an aeroplane that now spends its time hosting autonomous control software. The letters did not change. The subject did.

**The federal award record, which has not adopted the correction, is the only place the older claim survives at scale.** Whether the change of wording was a considered decision or an ordinary drift in a marketing department is not something the public record settles, and this article does not claim it was deliberate. **What is measured is that the two names differ, that the difference is exactly the word the acronym never contained, and that the money still uses the old one.**

## A Block Number That Means One Engine and a Cell That Names Another

**The one part of this register row that is not about simulation is the engines cell, and it contradicts the aeroplane's own block number.**

The row reads `1 Pratt & Whitney F100` \[[DOD 4120.15-L Addendum][ref_mds_addendum]\]. 27 of the 31 X rows carry an engines cell at all, and this is the only one naming that engine.

**The aeroplane is a Block 30, and the Air Force's own block convention says a Block 30 has a General Electric engine.** When the Alternate Fighter Engine programme brought a second supplier to the F-16 in the nineteen eighties, the two inlets and the two engines were distinguished by the last digit of the block number. **Blocks ending in zero take the General Electric F110 and blocks ending in two take the Pratt and Whitney F100** \[[General Dynamics F-16 Fighting Falcon][ref_f16]\] \[[General Electric F110][ref_f110]\] \[[Pratt and Whitney F100][ref_f100]\]. A Block 30 with an F100 is, by that convention, a contradiction in terms.

**Both statements are true and the resolution is that the aeroplane was re-engined.** It flew its thrust-vectoring work behind a General Electric F110-GE-100 fitted with an axisymmetric vectoring exhaust nozzle, completing 95 test flights before that programme ended in 1994 \[[X-62 Variable-Stability In-Flight Test Aircraft, Air and Space Forces Magazine weapons and platforms entry][ref_afa_x62]\]. A Pratt and Whitney thrust-vectoring nozzle and engine were installed next, that programme was cancelled, **and the aeroplane was converted to a standard F100-PW-229 and returned to its operators in June 1997** \[[F-16 VISTA, MATV and NF-16D, Variable-stability In-flight Simulator Test Aircraft, F-16.net][ref_f16net_vista]\]. The trade press records the same engine in its data table \[[X-62 Variable-Stability In-Flight Test Aircraft, Air and Space Forces Magazine weapons and platforms entry][ref_afa_x62]\].

**So the register's engines cell is right and the block number is right, and the two disagree because the aeroplane outlived the convention that named it.** This article does not claim to know what inlet the aeroplane now carries, which is the part of an engine change that a block number actually encodes, and the public record does not settle it.

**The rest of the airframe is assembled from three blocks as well.** The prime contractor describes it as a modified F-16D Block 30 Peace Marble Two aircraft upgraded with Block 40 avionics \[[VISTA X-62 Advancing Autonomy and Changing the Face of Air Power, Lockheed Martin, 13 February 2023][ref_lm_press]\], and the dorsal fairing that houses the variable-stability computers comes from the Israeli configuration, while the heavyweight landing gear is derived from the Block 40 and exists so that the aeroplane can simulate types with higher landing sink rates than an F-16 tolerates \[[General Dynamics X-62 VISTA][ref_x62_wikipedia]\].

**That last detail is the first sign of what this article is about.** A landing gear was changed not to improve the aeroplane but to widen the set of other aeroplanes it can pretend to be. **The modification is in the simulation's envelope rather than in the aircraft's.**

### The Letter It Carried Before the X

**Before 2021 the aeroplane was an NF-16D, and the N is a status prefix with a precise meaning.** It denotes special test, permanent, and it is applied when the modifications are so drastic that returning the aircraft to its original configuration, or converting it to a standard operational one, is beyond practicable or economic limits \[[X-62A and NF-16D VISTA, GlobalSecurity.org][ref_gs_x62]\] \[[Designations of U.S. Military Aircraft, including the modified mission and status prefix letters][ref_mds_aircraft]\].

**The N is therefore a stronger statement about the aeroplane than the X is.** The X says the aircraft is used for research. **The N says it can never go back.** The aeroplane carried the stronger letter for twenty-nine years and the weaker one for the last 4.48.

**And the X did not replace a claim about the aeroplane. It replaced a claim about its owner's intentions.** The school that operates it said at the time that the redesignation reflected the research done on the aircraft over nearly thirty years and acknowledged the upgrade programme then under way \[[X-62A and NF-16D VISTA, GlobalSecurity.org][ref_gs_x62]\]. **A redesignation that reflects the past is a different object from one that authorises a future**, and this series has met the second kind repeatedly and the first kind once.

## What the Variable Stability System Actually Commands

**The whole of this article's mathematics turns on one list, and the list is published.**

In-flight simulation on this aeroplane is done by a second flight control system running in parallel with the F-16's own, engaged once the aircraft is airborne, with a safety pilot in the back seat who can take control at any moment. **That second system commands, with essentially full authority, the left and right horizontal stabilators, the ailerons, the thrust, the rudder and the trailing-edge flaps** \[[X-62A and NF-16D VISTA, GlobalSecurity.org][ref_gs_x62]\]. The surfaces it does not command are the leading-edge flaps and the speedbrakes \[[F-16 VISTA, MATV and NF-16D, Variable-stability In-flight Simulator Test Aircraft, F-16.net][ref_f16net_vista]\].

**Count them by axis rather than by part number.** The two stabilators, driven together and driven differentially, are two independent controls rather than one, and so are the trailing-edge surfaces, which on an F-16 are flaperons and which the second system commands both symmetrically and asymmetrically \[[F-16 VISTA, MATV and NF-16D, Variable-stability In-flight Simulator Test Aircraft, F-16.net][ref_f16net_vista]\].

**That claim deserves its one line of algebra, because it is doing real work.** The symmetric and differential commands are a change of basis on the two surface deflections, and the matrix that performs it is invertible.

$$
\begin{bmatrix} \delta_s \\ \delta_d \end{bmatrix} = \tfrac{1}{2} \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 1 & -1 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} \delta_L \\ \delta_R \end{bmatrix} , \qquad \det = - \tfrac{1}{2} \ne 0
$$

**A non-zero determinant is the whole of the argument.** Two surfaces yield two independent commands exactly when the map between them can be undone, so the pair contributes two columns to the control effectiveness matrix rather than one. **A single all-moving tail, or two surfaces mechanically ganged, would contribute one**, and the next sections show what a missing column costs. So the system has **a symmetric stabilator, a symmetric flap and a throttle in the longitudinal axis**, and **a differential stabilator, an aileron and a rudder in the lateral-directional axis**. **3 in each.**

**An ordinary fighter pilot has 1 in pitch and 2 in roll and yaw.** The flaps are on a switch, the throttle is not part of the flight control system, and the stick moves one thing in pitch.

**That difference is not a matter of degree. The next section shows that it is the difference between a problem that has an exact solution and one that does not**, and the number 3 is not a coincidence.

## Model Following, Which Is the Mathematics of Pretending

**The programme's own name for what this aeroplane does is the Model Following Algorithm**, and the prime contractor lists it as a deliverable alongside the simulation system and the autonomy interface \[[VISTA X-62 Advancing Autonomy and Changing the Face of Air Power, Lockheed Martin, 13 February 2023][ref_lm_press]\] \[[Caraway, Harris and Cotting, VISTA X-62A Model Following Algorithm Overview, AIAA SciTech 2023][ref_scitech_mfa]\]. **The phrase is a term of art with a definition, a solvability condition and a computable failure, and all three are older than the aeroplane.**

### The Statement

Two linear systems are in play. The first is the host aeroplane, whose state is what the air and the metal actually do. The second is the model, which exists only inside a computer and which the host is required to imitate \[[Stevens, Lewis and Johnson, Aircraft Control and Simulation][book_stevens_lewis]\] \[[McRuer, Ashkenas and Graham, Aircraft Dynamics and Automatic Control][book_mcruer_dynamics]\].

$$
\dot{x} = A x + B u , \qquad \dot{x}_m = A_m x_m + B_m u_m
$$

The simulation is achieved by a control law that watches both systems and drives the host's surfaces \[[Model reference adaptive control][ref_mrac]\].

$$
u = K_x x + K_m x_m + K_u u_m
$$

Substituting one into the other gives the closed loop.

$$
\dot{x} = \left( A + B K_x \right) x + B K_m x_m + B K_u u_m
$$

**For the host's state to equal the model's state at every instant, given that the two start together, the closed loop must be the model.** Matching the two expressions term by term gives a pair of conditions on the gains.

$$
B \left( K_x + K_m \right) = A_m - A , \qquad B K_u = B_m
$$

**Notice what has happened. The unknowns are gains, the equations are linear in them, and the question is no longer about aeroplanes at all.** It is the question of whether two matrix equations have a solution, and that question has a standard answer.

### The Condition Is a Subspace Containment

A linear equation of the form $ B X = Y $ has an exact solution if and only if every column of $ Y $ lies in the column space of $ B $. The projector onto the complement of that column space is built from the Moore-Penrose pseudoinverse \[[Moore-Penrose inverse][ref_pseudoinverse]\] \[[Projection, the linear algebraic operation][ref_projection]\].

$$
\Pi = I - B B^{+}
$$

**And the conditions for exact model following are that this projector annihilates both right-hand sides.**

$$
\Pi \left( A_m - A \right) = 0 , \qquad \Pi B_m = 0
$$

**That is the whole of it, and it is the result a NASA Technical Memorandum of October 1967 states and proves** \[[Erzberger, Analysis and Design of Model Following Control Systems by State Space Techniques, NASA Technical Memorandum X-61189, 18 October 1967][ref_erzberger_1967]\]. When the conditions hold, the gains follow immediately, and they are the least-squares solution because in this case the least-squares solution is exact \[[Asseo, Application of Optimal Control to Perfect Model Following, Journal of Aircraft, 1970][ref_asseo_1970]\].

$$
K_x + K_m = B^{+} \left( A_m - A \right) , \qquad K_u = B^{+} B_m
$$

**That difference is the quantity the rest of this article is about, so it is worth a name.**

$$
\Delta A = A_m - A
$$

**Read the first condition in words.** The simulation demands a change of dynamics, being the difference between the model's dynamics matrix and the host's. **Every column of that difference must be producible by some combination of the host's controls.** The host's aerodynamics, its inertia, its speed and its altitude appear nowhere except through $ B $, and the model's realism appears nowhere except through $ A_m $. **The condition is about reach and not about power.**

### What It Costs When the Condition Fails

**The instrument was built on this literature and the literature knew it.** Calspan's other variable-stability aeroplane, the Total In-Flight Simulator, published its model-following system and the flight verification of it within five years of the memorandum \[[Pruner and Reynolds, The Total In-Flight Simulator Design and Capabilities, AIAA Simulation and Support Conference, 1968][ref_tifs_1968]\] \[[Motyka, Rynaski and Reynolds, Theory and Flight Verification of the TIFS Model-Following System, Journal of Aircraft, 1972][ref_tifs_1972]\]. **The mathematics and the aeroplanes that use it are the same generation**, and the X-62A is the fourth or fifth machine in that line rather than the first.

The literature calls the exact case **perfect model following** and the approximate case **real model following**, and it has done so since the nineteen seventies \[[Morrow and Balasubramanian, Real Model Following Control, Journal of Aircraft, 1975][ref_morrow_1975]\] \[[Lutze, A Perfect Explicit Model Following Control Solution to Imperfect Model Following Control Problems, AIAA Guidance, Navigation and Control Conference, 1989][ref_lutze_1989]\]. **The distinction is not a matter of tuning. It is a matter of whether a projector is zero.**

When it is not zero, the least-squares gains leave a residual.

$$
E = \Pi \left( A_m - A \right)
$$

And the error between the host and the model obeys an equation that is worth reading twice \[[Anderson and Schmidt, Error Dynamics and Perfect Model Following With Application to Flight Control, Journal of Guidance, Control, and Dynamics, 1991][ref_anderson_1991]\].

$$
\dot{e} = \left( A + B K_x \right) e + E x_m + \left( B K_u - B_m \right) u_m
$$

**Setting the derivative to zero says how large that error settles to**, and the expression contains the residual and nothing the designer can still choose.

$$
\dot{e} = 0 \quad \Longrightarrow \quad e_\infty = - \left( A + B K_x \right)^{-1} \Pi \, \Delta A \, x_m
$$

**The first term of the error equation is a stable homogeneous response and a designer can make it as fast as the hardware allows.** The second term is not. **It is driven by the model's own state**, which means that the harder the simulated aeroplane is manoeuvring, the larger the error, and no choice of $ K_x $ removes it because $ E $ does not contain $ K_x $. **A model-following error of this kind cannot be tuned away. It can only be designed away, by changing $ B $, which means by changing which surfaces the system is allowed to move.**

### The Counting Bound, Which Is the Design in One Line

The projector's rank is fixed by the rank of the control effectiveness matrix.

$$
\operatorname{rank} \Pi = n - \operatorname{rank} B \; \ge \; n - m
$$

**For the conditions to hold for an arbitrary model, the projector must be zero, and that requires the host's controls to span the whole state space.** Written out for each axis of an aeroplane, this is a counting statement about hardware.

| System | Dynamic states in the axis | Independent controls | Rank of the projector |
|---|---|---|---|
| An ordinary fighter, in pitch | 3 | 1 | 2 |
| An ordinary fighter, in roll and yaw | 3 | 2 | 1 |
| The variable stability system, in pitch | 3 | 3 | 0 |
| The variable stability system, in roll and yaw | 3 | 3 | 0 |

**The three dynamic states in the longitudinal axis are speed, angle of attack and pitch rate**, the pitch attitude being kinematic and therefore carried along by the others rather than needing to be commanded. The three in the lateral-directional axis are sideslip, roll rate and yaw rate, with bank angle kinematic in the same way.

**And the variable stability system has exactly three independent controls in each. That is not a coincidence and it is not generosity.** It is the smallest number that makes the projector vanish, and a system with two would face a one-dimensional subspace of demanded dynamics that no gain could produce.

**This is why the second flight control system commands the throttle.** A throttle is not a flight control on any fighter. It is here because the speed equation is one of the three and no aerodynamic surface on an F-16 can change the axial force independently of the normal force and the pitching moment. **The engine is not propulsion in this argument. It is the third column of a matrix.**

### The Bound Is Sufficient and Not Necessary, and Saying So Costs Nothing

**The counting above matches every state, and a simulation does not have to.** What the pilot is given is an output rather than a state, being an attitude, a rate, a load factor and whatever the instruments show, and matching an output is a weaker demand than matching everything behind it \[[Stevens, Lewis and Johnson, Aircraft Control and Simulation][book_stevens_lewis]\].

$$
y = C x \quad \Longrightarrow \quad \left( I - \left( C B \right) \left( C B \right)^{+} \right) C \, \Delta A = 0
$$

**The projector has shrunk.** It is now built from the product of the output matrix and the control matrix rather than from the control matrix alone, and that product has at most as many rows as there are outputs. **A simulation that only has to reproduce pitch rate and normal acceleration is asking for less than one that has to reproduce the whole state vector.**

**So three controls per axis is sufficient and it is not necessary**, and this article claims only the sufficiency. **What the weaker condition buys is a warning rather than a licence.** An output-matched simulation is exact in what the pilot is shown and free to be wrong in everything else, and the states it is free to be wrong in are still driving the aeroplane. **The mismatch does not disappear. It moves somewhere the pilot is not looking.**

### One Control Short, and Which Half of the Aeroplane Goes Wrong

**A rank deficiency of one sounds like a small defect and it is not, because the deficient direction is not distributed evenly over the aeroplane.**

Take the longitudinal short period alone, in the two states angle of attack and pitch rate, and ask a variable-stability system to turn a conventionally stable host into a statically unstable and lightly damped model. **That is the characteristic task**, because an aeroplane with dangerously poor flying qualities is exactly what a test pilot school wants its students to meet in a machine with a safety pilot in it \[[X-62A and NF-16D VISTA, GlobalSecurity.org][ref_gs_x62]\].

The short period in those two states has a standard form, and the one below is written with the angle-of-attack equation's pitch-rate coefficient set to unity, which is the usual normalisation \[[Etkin and Reid, Dynamics of Flight, Stability and Control][book_etkin_reid]\] \[[Cook, Flight Dynamics Principles][book_cook]\].

$$
\begin{bmatrix} \dot{\alpha} \\ \dot{q} \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} Z_\alpha & 1 \\ M_\alpha & M_q \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} \alpha \\ q \end{bmatrix}
$$

**A two-by-two matrix carries its own frequency and damping in its trace and its determinant**, so a pair of matrices can be read as two aeroplanes rather than as eight numbers.

$$
\omega_n = \sqrt{\det A} , \qquad 2 \zeta \omega_n = - \operatorname{tr} A
$$

**The numbers below are representative rather than measured.** The host and the model are plausible short-period pairs chosen to make the arithmetic legible, the control effectivenesses are in the ratio a horizontal tail and a trailing-edge flap actually stand in, and **nothing in the conclusion depends on the particular values**, only on the fact that a tail makes much more moment than lift and a flap makes much more lift than moment. The published F-16 aerodynamic data is tabular and graphical rather than closed form \[[Nguyen, Ogburn, Gilbert, Kibler, Brown and Deal, Simulator Study of Stall and Post-Stall Characteristics of a Fighter Airplane With Relaxed Longitudinal Static Stability, NASA Technical Paper 1538, December 1979][ref_tp1538]\], so this article does not claim to have computed the aeroplane's own matrices.

**Read through the relation above, the two matrices describe two quite different aeroplanes.** The host has a determinant of 9.8 per second squared, which is positive, so it is an ordinary oscillatory short period at **3.13 radians per second with a damping ratio of 0.431**, which is a damped period of 2.22 seconds. **The model's determinant is -1.76, which is negative**, and a negative determinant means the pair is not oscillatory at all.

$$
\det A < 0 \quad \Longrightarrow \quad \lambda = \tfrac{1}{2} \left( \operatorname{tr} A + \sqrt{\operatorname{tr}^2 A - 4 \det A} \right) > 0 , \qquad t_2 = \frac{\ln 2}{\lambda}
$$

**The model diverges, with a root of 0.918 per second and a time to double amplitude of 0.755 seconds.** That is the aeroplane the student is asked to fly, and the simulation's job is to move the determinant by 11.56 per second squared, from stable to divergent, using the surfaces of an aeroplane that is neither.

With two independent pitch controls the projector has rank 0 and the residual is zero to machine precision. **With the tail alone the projector has rank 1**, and a projector onto the complement of a single column has a closed form that makes the asymmetry visible before any arithmetic is done.

$$
\Pi = I - \frac{b \, b^{\mathrm{T}}}{b^{\mathrm{T}} b}
$$

**The projector removes the direction the control points in and leaves everything perpendicular to it untouched.** A tail column points almost entirely along the pitching-moment axis, so what survives the projector is almost entirely the lift axis. **The residual is therefore not spread over the problem.** Writing the surviving fraction row by row says so in numbers.

$$
\eta_\alpha = \frac{\left\| \left( \Pi \, \Delta A \right)_\alpha \right\|}{\left\| \Delta A_\alpha \right\|} , \qquad \eta_q = \frac{\left\| \left( \Pi \, \Delta A \right)_q \right\|}{\left\| \Delta A_q \right\|}
$$

| Row of the dynamics matrix | Change demanded | Change unreachable | Fraction unreachable |
|---|---|---|---|
| Angle of attack | 0.6 per second | 0.5 per second | 83.3 percent |
| Pitch rate | 10.06 per second squared | 0.005 per second squared | 0.05 percent |

**With one pitch control the pitch-damping row can be retuned almost exactly and the lift row cannot be touched at all.** The ratio between the two failures is 1,677.

**That is not a numerical curiosity. It is the physical content of the whole design.** A horizontal tail is a moment generator. Deflected, it changes how the aeroplane rotates and it barely changes how much lift the aeroplane makes. **So a simulator built round a tail alone can imitate any pitch stiffness and any pitch damping it likes, and it cannot imitate a different wing.**

**The quantity that stays the host's own is the one the pilot feels in the seat.**

$$
\frac{n_z}{\alpha} = \frac{\bar{q} \, S \, C_{L_\alpha}}{W}
$$

**Every term on the right belongs to the host.** The dynamic pressure is the host's speed and altitude, the area is the host's wing and the slope is the host's aerodynamics. **A pitch control changes none of them**, so the acceleration a given angle of attack produces is whatever the F-16 produces, whatever the model says it should be.

**And the error a single control leaves does not decay.** For a steady one-radian angle of attack demanded of the model, the residual drives a steady angle-of-attack error of **7.6 percent** and a steady pitch-rate error of 0.409 per second. **A student flying that simulation is holding a different angle of attack from the one the model is holding, permanently, and no gain in the system removes it.**

**A symmetric trailing-edge flap is the missing column.** It makes lift with comparatively little moment, and adding it to the matrix takes the unreachable subspace from one dimension to none. **The variable stability system commands the trailing-edge flaps for exactly this reason**, and the reason is visible in the arithmetic before any document says so.

## The Determinant Is a Distance

**Two lifting controls only count as two if they act at different places, and the determinant says so in a form that has no aerodynamics in it.**

A control surface that produces a normal force at a station aft of the centre of gravity produces a pitching moment in proportion, with the moment arm measured in mean aerodynamic chords \[[Etkin and Reid, Dynamics of Flight, Stability and Control][book_etkin_reid]\] \[[Nelson, Flight Stability and Automatic Control][book_nelson]\].

$$
M_f = - \frac{\ell_f}{\bar{c}} Z_f , \qquad M_h = - \frac{\ell_h}{\bar{c}} Z_h
$$

Substituting into the two-by-two block that maps the two lifting controls onto normal force and pitching moment gives a determinant that collapses.

$$
\det \begin{bmatrix} Z_f & Z_h \\ M_f & M_h \end{bmatrix} = \frac{Z_f Z_h}{\bar{c}} \left( \ell_f - \ell_h \right)
$$

**The control effectivenesses appear as a product and the geometry appears as a difference.** Make either surface twice as powerful and the determinant doubles. **Move the two surfaces to the same station and the determinant is zero however powerful they are**, because two forces applied at one point are one force.

**Independent command of lift and pitching moment is therefore a fact about where the surfaces are**, and the quantity that decides it is the separation between their centres of pressure measured in chords. For an F-16, with the flap on the wing trailing edge and the tail well aft, that separation is of order 0.6 chords.

**Conditioning is what the determinant understates.** A matrix can be invertible and still useless, because the deflections required to achieve a given change scale with the inverse of its smallest singular value \[[Condition number][ref_condition_number]\] \[[Singular value decomposition][ref_singular_value]\].

$$
\kappa = \frac{\sigma_{\max}}{\sigma_{\min}}
$$

**The relation behind that sentence is worth displaying, because the article has so far treated deflection as free and it is the scarcest thing the aeroplane has.** The gains solve the matching condition, the deflection is the gains acting on the state, and the worst case over states of a given size is bounded by the demanded change divided by the smallest singular value.

$$
u = \left( K_x + K_m \right) x , \qquad \left\| K_x + K_m \right\| \le \frac{\left\| \Delta A \right\|}{\sigma_{\min} \left( B \right)}
$$

| Separation between the two lifting controls | Condition number |
|---|---|
| 0.6 chords, being the order of the actual layout | 7.17 |
| Half of that | 12.13 |
| Two hundredths of a chord, being effectively coincident | 157.8 |

**Halving the separation worsens the conditioning by a factor of 1.69**, and driving it to zero sends the condition number through two orders of magnitude on its way to infinity. **The deflections required to simulate a given aeroplane grow in the same proportion**, and the next section shows that deflection is precisely the resource this aeroplane runs out of.

**The separation is a property of the airframe and nothing in the simulation software can change it.** A variable-stability aeroplane whose lifting controls happened to sit close together would be a poor instrument no matter how good its computers were, and the arithmetic says by how much.

### The Column That Makes the Projector Vanish Is the Column That Runs Out First

**Solving the worked example for its gains rather than for its residual gives a result the rank argument does not predict.**

The simulation of the previous section demands **0.82 degrees of symmetric tail and 2.63 degrees of symmetric flap for every degree of angle of attack.** Both are gradients rather than deflections, and the quotient is what matters. **The flap is asked for more than three times as much**, because it is the weaker lift producer of the two and it is being asked to supply all of the change in lift.

| Surface | Demanded by a five-degree excursion | Published limit | Share of the limit |
|---|---|---|---|
| Symmetric horizontal tail | 4.09 degrees | 25 degrees | 16.4 percent |
| Symmetric flap | 13.16 degrees | 21.5 degrees | 61.2 percent |

**The flap is 3.74 times closer to its stops than the tail is to its own.** Carrying the excursion up until something saturates, **the flap reaches its limit at 8.17 degrees of angle of attack and the tail would not reach its own until 30.5 degrees**.

**That reverses the intuition the rank argument leaves.** The tail is the powerful surface and the flap is the afterthought, and the counting bound says only that the flap must be there. **The deflection arithmetic says the flap is what runs out**, so the envelope of aeroplanes this machine can imitate is set by its weakest control rather than by its strongest.

**The bound of the previous relation is loose here and that is worth saying.** It gives 53.4 against a realised gain norm of 2.76, a factor of 19.4, because the worst-case direction the bound assumes is not the direction this particular simulation demands. **A bound that is loose by a factor of nineteen is a bound and not an estimate**, and the realised value is the one the table above uses.

## The Frequency at Which the Simulation Runs Out of Authority Is Published

**NASA released the numbers that bound this aeroplane's simulation in 1979, twelve years before it flew as a simulator, in a report that never names the type in its title.**

Technical Paper 1538 studies the stall and post-stall behaviour of a fighter with relaxed longitudinal static stability, and says in its appendix on aerodynamic data that the data came from low-speed wind-tunnel tests of subscale models of the F-16 \[[Nguyen, Ogburn, Gilbert, Kibler, Brown and Deal, Simulator Study of Stall and Post-Stall Characteristics of a Fighter Airplane With Relaxed Longitudinal Static Stability, NASA Technical Paper 1538, December 1979][ref_tp1538]\]. Its Table 1 gives the mass, the inertias, the wing geometry and the surface deflection limits. **Its Appendix A gives the actuator lag and the rate limit of every surface**, and those two numbers are what decide how fast a simulation can be.

### A Rate Limit Is a Frequency in Disguise

A surface commanded to oscillate must move fastest as it passes through zero, and the peak rate is the product of the amplitude and the frequency \[[Slew rate][ref_slew_rate]\].

$$
\delta \left( t \right) = \hat{\delta} \sin \omega t \qquad \Longrightarrow \qquad \left| \dot{\delta} \right|_{\max} = \hat{\delta} \omega \le R
$$

**Divide the rate limit by the deflection limit and the result has the dimensions of a frequency.** It is the highest frequency at which the surface can still reach its stops.

$$
\omega_c = \frac{R}{\delta_{\max}}
$$

Above it the usable amplitude falls as the reciprocal of frequency, so the fraction of authority available is a simple ratio \[[Describing function][ref_describing_function]\].

$$
\frac{\hat{\delta} \left( \omega \right)}{\delta_{\max}} = \min \left( 1 , \frac{\omega_c}{\omega} \right)
$$

**At the short period, for any surface whose corner frequency falls below it, that ratio is the whole of the answer.**

$$
\frac{\hat{\delta} \left( \omega_{sp} \right)}{\delta_{\max}} = \frac{\omega_c}{\omega_{sp}} \qquad \text{whenever} \qquad \omega_c < \omega_{sp}
$$

**These are the published limits, with the corner frequency computed from the two columns beside it.**

| Surface | Deflection limit | Rate limit | Full-deflection corner | Commanded by the second system |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Symmetric horizontal tail | 25.0 degrees | 60.0 degrees per second | 2.40 radians per second | yes |
| Differential horizontal tail, per surface | 5.375 degrees | 60.0 degrees per second | 11.16 radians per second | yes |
| Aileron, which is a flaperon on this aircraft | 21.5 degrees | 80.0 degrees per second | 3.72 radians per second | yes |
| Rudder | 30.0 degrees | 120.0 degrees per second | 4.00 radians per second | yes |
| Leading-edge flap, which the second system does not command | 25.0 degrees | 25.0 degrees per second | 1.00 radians per second | no |

**Read the fourth column and the design becomes visible.**

**The symmetric horizontal tail, which has the most deflection of any surface commanded by the second system, has the lowest corner frequency of all of them at 2.4 radians per second**, which is 0.382 hertz. **That is below the short-period frequency of the aeroplanes this machine exists to imitate.** A fighter short period sits in the region of 4 radians per second, and at that frequency the stabilator can reach only 60 percent of its travel, which is 15 degrees out of twenty-five.

**The differential tail is the opposite case and the contrast is exact.** It has the least deflection of any of them and the same rate limit as the stabilator, so its corner frequency is higher by precisely the ratio of the two deflection limits, 4.65 against 4.65. **The surface with a fifth of the authority has more than four times the bandwidth at full authority**, and at the short period it is not rate limited at all.

**A designer who had sized the rate limits in proportion to the deflections would have produced the same corner frequency everywhere.** That did not happen. The rate limits run 60, 60, 80 and 120 degrees per second against deflections of 25, 5.375, 21.5 and 30, and **the four corner frequencies come out at 2.4, 11.16, 3.72 and 4 radians per second**, a spread of nearly five to one.

**This article does not know why.** The limits were set for a fighter and not for a simulator, twenty years before the simulator existed, and the second flight control system inherited them. **What can be said is that the inheritance is uneven and that the unevenness falls on the axis that matters most**, because pitch is where a variable-stability aeroplane does most of its work and the pitch surface is the slowest of the four.

### The Leading-Edge Flap Is the Cheapest Column Nobody Bought

**The leading-edge flap has a corner frequency of exactly 1 radian per second**, being twenty-five degrees of travel at twenty-five degrees per second, and its actuator lag is 2.75 times longer than every other surface's \[[Nguyen, Ogburn, Gilbert, Kibler, Brown and Deal, Simulator Study of Stall and Post-Stall Characteristics of a Fighter Airplane With Relaxed Longitudinal Static Stability, NASA Technical Paper 1538, December 1979][ref_tp1538]\]. **It is also a direct lift device, which makes it, on paper, a fourth column for the longitudinal control matrix.**

**And the second flight control system does not command it.** The published account of what the system drives lists the trailing-edge flaps and omits the leading-edge ones \[[F-16 VISTA, MATV and NF-16D, Variable-stability In-flight Simulator Test Aircraft, F-16.net][ref_f16net_vista]\].

**The arithmetic above is a sufficient reason and this article offers it as a reading rather than as a finding.** A surface that can reach only 25 percent of its travel at the short-period frequency, through an actuator 2.75 times slower than the others, adds a column to the matrix that is almost empty in the band where the simulation lives.

**The second reason is that the surface is already spoken for, and the schedule that speaks for it is published in the same appendix as the actuator lag.**

$$
\delta_l = 1.38 \, \frac{2 s + \omega_p}{s + \omega_p} \, \alpha - 9.05 \, \frac{\bar{q}}{P_s} + 1.45 , \qquad \omega_p = 7.25
$$

**Read the three terms.** A lead network on angle of attack, a subtraction proportional to the ratio of dynamic to static pressure, and a constant bias. The network passes 1.38 degrees of flap per degree of angle of attack in steady flight and asks for 2.76 above its own pole, because its numerator's coefficient of the Laplace variable is twice its denominator's. **It is a lead of two, with a zero at 3.625 and a pole at 7.25 radians per second.**

**And the actuator that has to execute it has a corner of 7.35 radians per second**, which is 1.42 percent from the schedule's own pole. Putting the two in series says what the surface actually does.

$$
\frac{\delta_l \left( s \right)}{\alpha \left( s \right)} = 1.38 \, \frac{2 s + \omega_p}{s + \omega_p} \cdot \frac{1}{\tau_l s + 1} , \qquad \omega_p \tau_l = 0.986
$$

**The product of the schedule's pole and the actuator's time constant is 0.986.** If the two corners coincided exactly it would be one. **They very nearly do**, so the pole the network introduces and the pole the hardware introduces sit on top of one another, and above that frequency the combined response has one zero and two poles and therefore falls rather than rises.

| Quantity | Between one and fifteen radians per second |
|---|---|
| Gain rise the schedule commands | 1.8 |
| Gain rise the surface delivers | 0.8 |
| Shortfall | 2.25 |

**The schedule asks the flap to become nearly twice as active across that band and the flap becomes slightly less active**, and by fifteen radians per second the combined response lags by 51.7 degrees. **The lead is not merely reduced. Its sign is reversed.**

**This article does not claim that the coincidence was deliberate or that anyone has noticed it.** The schedule was designed for an aeroplane and the actuator was sized for a surface, and a near-cancellation between two poles chosen twenty years apart is as likely to be an accident as a design. **What can be said is that the surface the simulation might have wanted is already carrying a command it cannot execute**, which is a third reason on top of the two the previous paragraphs give, and the public record does not say which of the three governed.

## The Actuator Puts a Floor Under Every Aeroplane This One Can Be

**The most important consequence of the published numbers is not a limit on authority. It is a limit on quickness, and it is one-sided.**

Every surface but the leading-edge flap is modelled as a first-order lag of 0.0495 seconds \[[Nguyen, Ogburn, Gilbert, Kibler, Brown and Deal, Simulator Study of Stall and Post-Stall Characteristics of a Fighter Airplane With Relaxed Longitudinal Static Stability, NASA Technical Paper 1538, December 1979][ref_tp1538]\].

$$
\frac{\delta \left( s \right)}{\delta_c \left( s \right)} = \frac{1}{\tau s + 1} , \qquad \omega_a = \frac{1}{\tau}
$$

That corner frequency is 20.2 radians per second, or 3.22 hertz, and the phase it costs grows with frequency.

$$
\varphi \left( \omega \right) = - \arctan \left( \omega \tau \right)
$$

**At the short period it is 11.2 degrees**, and at low frequency the lag behaves as a pure time delay of the same time constant.

$$
\frac{1}{\tau s + 1} \; \simeq \; e^{- \tau s} \qquad \text{whenever} \qquad \omega \tau \ll 1
$$

**The approximation is very good across the band this article uses.** The phase a first-order lag contributes differs from a pure delay's by 0.018 of a degree at two radians per second, 0.145 at four and 1.086 at eight. **So calling the actuator a delay of 49.5 milliseconds is a statement about the hardware and not a convenience.**

**Now consider what a model-following system is.** It reads a command, computes what the model would do, and moves the host's surfaces to make the host do it. **Every delay in the host therefore sits between the pilot's hand and the simulated response**, and equivalent delays in series add.

$$
\tau_e \left( \text{host and model} \right) = \tau_e \left( \text{host} \right) + \tau_e \left( \text{model} \right) \; \ge \; \tau_e \left( \text{host} \right)
$$

**That inequality is the whole of the argument and it has no escape in it.** Both terms are non-negative, so the sum is at least the first, and the first belongs to an aeroplane built in the nineteen eighties.

$$
\tau_s \; \ge \; \tau + \frac{3}{2 f_s}
$$

**A variable-stability aeroplane can make any aeroplane sluggish and it cannot make any aeroplane crisp.** It can add lag, it can add instability, it can add a hundred milliseconds of transport delay and show a student what that feels like. **It cannot subtract its own hardware.** The set of aeroplanes it can faithfully reproduce is bounded below, and the bound is the host's own equivalent delay.

**The floor is at least 49.5 milliseconds from the actuator alone.** A digital implementation adds sampling and transport. **Assuming a frame rate of sixty hertz**, which this article assumes and does not know, the computation contributes half a frame of sampling and one frame of transport, which is a further 16.7 and 16.7 halved, **for a floor of about 74.5 milliseconds and 17.1 degrees of phase at the short period**.

**The frame rate is an assumption and the article flags it as one.** The actuator number is published and the conclusion does not depend on the assumed part, because a floor of forty-nine and a half milliseconds is already a floor. **What the assumption buys is an order of magnitude for the computational share, and the order of magnitude is that it is comparable to the hardware rather than negligible beside it.**

## The Instrument Shares the Failure Mode of the Thing It Studies

**A rate-limited actuator is the standard mechanism of one class of pilot-induced oscillation, and this aeroplane's actuators are rate limited.**

Pilot-induced oscillation, which the field increasingly calls aircraft-pilot coupling because the pilot is rarely the cause, is an unstable oscillation of the closed loop formed by a human operator and an aircraft \[[Pilot-induced oscillation][ref_pio]\] \[[McRuer and Krendel, Mathematical Models of Human Pilot Behavior][book_mcruer_pilot]\]. **The linear case is understood and designed against.** The category that has been hardest to predict is the one in which the aircraft is linear until a surface hits its rate limit, at which point the effective phase lag jumps and a loop that was stable a moment earlier is not.

**The mechanism is the describing function of the rate limiter**, which is the effective gain a nonlinear element presents to a sinusoid of a given amplitude and frequency \[[Describing function][ref_describing_function]\] \[[Slotine and Li, Applied Nonlinear Control][book_slotine]\].

**A rate limiter deep in saturation is moving at its limit throughout the cycle**, so its output is not a distorted sinusoid but a triangle, and the triangle's amplitude follows from the limit and the frequency alone.

$$
\left| \dot{\delta} \right| = R \quad \Longrightarrow \quad \hat{\delta}_o = \frac{\pi R}{2 \omega}
$$

The fundamental of a triangular wave is eight over pi squared times its amplitude, so the gain the element presents is the quotient of that fundamental and the input.

$$
\left| N \right| = \frac{8}{\pi^2} \cdot \frac{\hat{\delta}_o}{\hat{\delta}} = \frac{4 R}{\pi \, \hat{\delta} \, \omega}
$$

**The gain falls as the reciprocal of frequency and as the reciprocal of amplitude**, which is an amplitude-dependent bandwidth and is exactly what makes the phenomenon hard to predict from a linear model. **The tighter the pilot tries to control, the larger the command and the smaller the gain the aeroplane returns.** That is a positive feedback between effort and difficulty, and it is why the phenomenon appears in demanding tasks and is absent in gentle ones.

| Condition | Onset ratio | Triangular output | Gain | Amplitude lost |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Full tail travel at the short period | 0.6 | 23.56 degrees | 0.764 | 23.6 percent |
| Full tail travel at ten radians per second | 0.24 | 9.42 degrees | 0.306 | 69.4 percent |

**The relation above is the deep-saturation asymptote and not the describing function itself, and the clearest evidence for that is that it exceeds one at onset.** Evaluated where the demanded rate exactly equals the limit it gives 1.273, and a rate limiter cannot amplify. **The true describing function is continuous and equals one there**, so the figures in the first row of that table, taken near onset, are indicative rather than exact, while the second row is well inside the asymptote's range.

**And the phase is the part this article cannot supply.** An ideal rate limiter, one that simply clips the slope of its input, is an even operation on an odd input and contributes no phase lag at all. **The phase lag that makes this phenomenon dangerous comes from the servo loop wrapped around the limiter**, which is what a real actuator is, and its size depends on the loop gain and the loop's own dynamics. **This article has the actuator's lag and its rate limit and does not have its loop**, so it reports the gain loss and declines to quote a phase.

**A variable-stability aeroplane exists in part to study this**, because putting a student in a machine that can be made to oscillate under a safety pilot's supervision is safer than discovering the property on a prototype. The school that operates this aircraft says so directly, describing its purpose as giving students the opportunity to practise testing aircraft with dangerously poor flying qualities \[[X-62A and NF-16D VISTA, GlobalSecurity.org][ref_gs_x62]\].

**And the instrument contains the nonlinearity it is used to investigate.** The second flight control system drives the same surfaces through the same actuators with the same published rate limits. **When the simulated aeroplane demands a stabilator motion beyond 2.4 radians per second at full travel, the host rate limits**, and the phase that costs is added to the simulated response. **The student meets a lag that belongs to the host rather than to the model, and nothing in the cockpit distinguishes the two.**

**This is not a criticism of the aeroplane. It is a statement of what an in-flight simulator is.** Every simulator of every kind has this property, and the reason a flying one is preferred to a ground-based one is that its unmodelled remainder is an aeroplane rather than a motion platform. **The remainder is still there.** The honest formulation is that the machine simulates the model plus itself, that the sum is what the pilot rates, and that separating the two is a question about the instrument rather than about the aeroplane under study.

**The published limits say where the separation matters.** Below 2.4 radians per second at full stabilator travel, and proportionately higher at smaller amplitudes, the host's rate limits are not active and the simulation is whatever the linear analysis says it is. **Above them the host is contributing a nonlinearity of its own**, and a result obtained there is a result about a particular F-16 with a particular set of hydraulic actuators.

### What the Delay Floor Costs the Pilot

**The strongest single result in manual control theory is that a trained operator adapts until the open loop looks like an integrator near the frequency at which the loop gain passes unity** \[[McRuer and Krendel, Mathematical Models of Human Pilot Behavior][book_mcruer_pilot]\] \[[McRuer, Ashkenas and Graham, Aircraft Dynamics and Automatic Control][book_mcruer_dynamics]\].

$$
Y_p \left( s \right) Y_c \left( s \right) \; \simeq \; \frac{\omega_{co} \, e^{- \tau_e s}}{s}
$$

**The consequence is that the pilot supplies whatever the aeroplane lacks, and the one thing no adaptation supplies is phase.** An integrator alone leaves ninety degrees of margin at crossover, and a transport delay eats into it linearly.

$$
\varphi_m = \frac{\pi}{2} - \omega_{co} \tau_e
$$

**So the delay floor is a fixed tax on the pilot's margin, charged before the simulated aeroplane has contributed anything.**

| At a crossover of | The actuator alone costs | The floor costs | Leaving |
|---|---|---|---|
| Three radians per second | 8.51 degrees | 12.81 degrees | 77.19 degrees |
| Six radians per second | 17.02 degrees | 25.61 degrees | 64.39 degrees |

**At the middle of the range the crossover model reports for compensatory tracking, the host consumes 14.23 percent of the available margin. At the upper end it consumes 28.46 percent.** The crossover frequencies are assumed and are named as assumptions. **The delay is published.**

**Setting the margin to zero gives the frequency at which the host's own hardware forbids a loop closure outright.**

$$
\varphi_m = 0 \quad \Longrightarrow \quad \omega_{co} = \frac{\pi}{2 \tau_e}
$$

**That is 21.08 radians per second for the floor and 31.73 for the actuator alone.** Both are far above where a human pilot works, **so the ceiling is not the binding constraint and this article does not claim it is.** What binds is the tax, which is paid at every crossover frequency and which the simulation cannot refund.

## The Answer Comes Back on an Ordinal Scale

**Whatever this aeroplane measures, it reports through a human being, and the reporting scale has a property that bounds what can be done with the answer.**

The standard instrument is the Cooper-Harper rating scale, which is a decision tree ending in ten numbered boxes \[[Cooper-Harper rating scale][ref_cooper_harper]\] \[[Hodgkinson, Aircraft Handling Qualities][book_hodgkinson]\]. A pilot answers a sequence of questions about whether the aircraft is controllable, whether adequate performance is attainable, and what compensation is required, and arrives at a number between one and ten. **The numbers are ordered and the ordering is meaningful.** A rating of three describes an aeroplane better than a rating of five.

**The spacing is not meaningful, and that is a property of the scale rather than an opinion about it** \[[Level of measurement][ref_ordinal]\]. There is no sense in which the distance from three to five equals the distance from six to eight. The boundaries between the three handling-qualities levels fall between ratings three and four and between six and seven, and those two boundaries are the scale's only claims about magnitude. **The other seven gaps assert nothing.**

**The formal statement is about which transformations of the scale leave it saying the same thing.** An ordinal scale is one whose content survives any strictly increasing relabelling of its points.

$$
r_1 < r_2 \; \iff \; g \left( r_1 \right) < g \left( r_2 \right) \qquad \text{for every strictly increasing } g
$$

**So a statistic is meaningful on such a scale exactly when it commutes with every such relabelling**, and that single test separates the summaries that are allowed from the summaries that are not.

$$
\operatorname{med} \left( g \left( r \right) \right) = g \left( \operatorname{med} \left( r \right) \right) , \qquad \operatorname{mean} \left( g \left( r \right) \right) \ne g \left( \operatorname{mean} \left( r \right) \right)
$$

**The median is the middle element and relabelling the elements does not change which one is in the middle.** The mean is a sum divided by a count, and a sum depends on the distances between the labels, which is precisely what an ordinal scale declines to supply.

**The consequence is that a mean pilot rating is a category error.** So is a standard deviation of pilot ratings, and so is any statistical procedure that assumes the intervals are equal. **The defensible summaries are the median, the range and the counts in each level**, and the defensible tests are rank-based ones.

**The practice of averaging is nonetheless widespread**, and this article is not in a position to say how widespread, because that would require reading a sample of the handling-qualities literature large enough to support the claim and this survey has not done it. **What can be said is that the scale's own definition forbids it**, that the alternative is not difficult, and that an instrument whose output is ordinal cannot be made interval by the precision of the aeroplane feeding it.

**This is the sharpest limit in the article and it is not a limit on the aeroplane at all.** The model-following condition is exact, the residual is computable, the rate limits are published, the delay floor is arithmetic. **And the quantity all of that machinery exists to deliver is a number a human being picks out of ten boxes.** The instrument is far more precise than its own readout, which is an unusual place for an engineering system to be and worth stating plainly rather than leaving implied.

## What It Costs to Keep an Instrument Flying

**The previous two articles read a contract record that paid for a development programme. This one reads a contract record that pays rent on an aeroplane, and that is a different object.**

The X-60A's money outlived its publicity by three years and ended by paying to ship equipment. The X-61A's money stopped forty-seven days after the flight that mattered while the period of performance ran on for another four years. **Neither of those shapes appears here.** This record runs in calendar-year increments to two contractors for more than a decade, and it therefore answers a question the other two could not, which is what an in-flight simulator costs to own.

**73 transactions across 18 awards total 29,085,924.37 dollars**, from 21 February 2014 to 30 September 2025, a span of 11.6 years \[[USAspending][ref_usaspending]\].

**Every total in this section is a reassembly and not a restatement**, which is a distinction worth one line of notation because the whole reliability of the section rests on it.

$$
\sum_k v_k = V
$$

**The registry publishes the left side and the right side independently.** The transactions are filed one at a time by the contracting office as money moves and the award total is a separate field. **Agreement between them is therefore evidence for both, and disagreement would be a defect in one**, which is a stronger position than quoting either alone. **17 of the 18 agree to the cent.** The one that does not is excluded because part of it falls past this article's date.

| Calendar year | Obligated | Share of the total |
|---|---|---|
| 2014 | 514,070.00 dollars | 1.8 percent |
| 2015 | 653,933.00 dollars | 2.2 percent |
| 2016 | 56,620.01 dollars | 0.2 percent |
| 2018 | 3,946,393.66 dollars | 13.6 percent |
| 2019 | 10,000.00 dollars | 0.0 percent |
| 2020 | 1,843,037.33 dollars | 6.3 percent |
| 2021 | 6,020,876.27 dollars | 20.7 percent |
| 2022 | 6,183,543.77 dollars | 21.3 percent |
| 2023 | 3,816,669.74 dollars | 13.1 percent |
| 2024 | 840,780.59 dollars | 2.9 percent |
| 2025 | 5,200,000.00 dollars | 17.9 percent |
| **All years** | **29,085,924.37 dollars** | **100.0 percent** |

**Two contractors hold all of it.** Calspan takes 23,611,921.77 dollars, which is 81.2 percent, and Lockheed Martin takes 5,474,002.60 dollars, which is 18.8 percent. **The split follows the division of labour the press releases describe**, with the simulation system belonging to the laboratory and the airframe and the autonomy interface to the prime contractor \[[VISTA X-62 Advancing Autonomy and Changing the Face of Air Power, Lockheed Martin, 13 February 2023][ref_lm_press]\].

### The Redesignation Is Visible in the Money

**Obligations run at 1,390,629.73 dollars a year before 14 June 2021 and 4,404,494.90 dollars a year after it, a ratio of 3.17.**

**The average over the whole record is 2,506,165.10 dollars a year, and quoting that alone would conceal the thing worth reporting.** It is the figure a reader would compute first and it is 1.76 times smaller than the rate the aeroplane has actually been running at since the redesignation.

**That is a comparison of averages over unequal periods and it should be read as one.** The earlier period includes two years with almost no obligations at all and one, 2018, with nearly four million. **The step is real and the smoothness is not**, and an aeroplane bought a calendar year at a time will always show a lumpy record.

**The first obligation after the redesignation came 31 days later**, being 1,350,000.00 dollars for the third phase of the simulation system upgrade \[[Contract FA930421F5020, VISTA Simulation System upgrade Phase III, Department of the Air Force to Calspan][ref_usa_vss3]\]. **The redesignation and the upgrade are the same event seen from two records.**

**And the largest single obligation in the whole twelve years is the most recent one.** 5,200,000.00 dollars were obligated on 30 September 2025, which is 17.9 percent of everything and falls 68 days before this article's date. **It is dated the last day of a fiscal year**, which is where a great deal of federal money moves and which this article notes without inferring anything from it.

**The record also carries 22 modifications obligating nothing and 5 deobligating a total of 68,585.40 dollars.** A zero-dollar modification is an administrative action against an open award and is a different object from spending, which is a distinction the previous article established and this record confirms.

**6 transactions fall after this article's date and are excluded at the source rather than in the prose**, carrying 782,854.00 dollars between them. **One of those is the only place in the entire record where the designation X-62A appears**, which is why the exclusion is not a formality. An article that filtered in the sentence rather than in the data would have reported the opposite of this record's most interesting property.

### The Register's Unofficial Sentence Is Corroborated by a Different Government Record

**The compiler marks the X-62A's description as not official Department of Defense wording, and the description says the upgrade was for the Skyborg programme** \[[DOD 4120.15-L Addendum][ref_mds_addendum]\]. **That is a reconstruction from open sources and the compiler says so.**

**The contract record confirms it independently.** 108 days after the redesignation, the Air Force obligated 799,956.00 dollars to Lockheed Martin under a line whose description names **HAVE Autonomous Air Combat Operations Phase Two Skyborg** \[[Contract FA930421F5034, HAVE Autonomous Air Combat Operations Phase II Skyborg, Department of the Air Force to Lockheed Martin][ref_usa_haveaaco]\]. The word appears 73 transactions into a record that never once uses the designation.

**This is worth stating carefully because it is an epistemic result and not a factual one.** The previous article could establish that the register had stopped being a primary source and could not do anything about it. **This one can, for one sentence, because the accounting system and the designation register are independent records maintained for unrelated purposes** and they agree. **That does not make the sentence official. It makes it corroborated**, which is a weaker claim and a more useful one.

## The Autonomy the Number Was For

**The programme the redesignation served has a stated challenge problem and it is not flying.** The agency describes its Air Combat Evolution effort as seeking to increase trust in combat autonomy by using human-machine collaborative dogfighting as its challenge problem, and says that in parallel it will implement methods to measure, calibrate, increase and predict human trust in that autonomy \[[ACE, Air Combat Evolution, Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency programme page][ref_darpa_ace]\].

**Trust is the deliverable and the dogfight is the test case.** That ordering is unusual enough to be worth dwelling on. The stated aim is a hierarchical division in which a human keeps the high-level decisions, being the engagement strategy, the choice and priority of targets and the weapon or effect, while the machine keeps the details of manoeuvre and tactics \[[ACE, Air Combat Evolution, Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency programme page][ref_darpa_ace]\]. **The pilot is to become a mission commander, and the aeroplane's role is to make that division credible enough to be trusted.**

**The aircraft was flown by an artificial intelligence agent for more than seventeen hours in December 2022**, which the prime contractor described at the time as the first occasion on which such an agent had been engaged on a tactical aircraft \[[VISTA X-62 Advancing Autonomy and Changing the Face of Air Power, Lockheed Martin, 13 February 2023][ref_lm_press]\]. The trade press records the same campaign as twenty-one flights and describes the aircraft as the first supersonic aeroplane to fly under such control, progressing to engagements against crewed fighters in 2023 \[[X-62 Variable-Stability In-Flight Test Aircraft, Air and Space Forces Magazine weapons and platforms entry][ref_afa_x62]\].

**All of these are claims by interested parties and this article reports them as such.** The agency, the prime contractor and the school all have reasons to describe the result as a first. **Nothing in this survey's 8,579 records contradicts any of them**, which is a statement about what was searched rather than about what is true.

### The Same Three Controls, and Why the Autonomy Fits

**What makes this aeroplane useful for autonomy work is the property established four sections ago**, and it is not obvious from the press releases.

An autonomous agent developed for an uncrewed aircraft is written against that aircraft's dynamics. **To fly it on a host, the host must present the agent with the dynamics it expects**, which is model following with the model supplied by whichever vehicle the agent was built for. **The upgrade programme added a system for autonomous control of the simulation on top of the existing simulation system**, together with the model-following algorithm itself \[[VISTA X-62 Advancing Autonomy and Changing the Face of Air Power, Lockheed Martin, 13 February 2023][ref_lm_press]\] \[[Cotting, Stephens, Cole, Barricklow and Gray, X-62 VISTA Capabilities and Architecture, AIAA SciTech 2023][ref_scitech_capabilities]\].

**So the agent commands a simulated aeroplane, the simulation runs on a real one, and a safety pilot sits behind both.** The projector being zero is what makes the middle layer honest, and the statement it licenses is an equality between transfer functions rather than a resemblance.

$$
\Pi = 0 \quad \Longrightarrow \quad G_{cl} \left( s \right) = C \left( s I - A_m \right)^{-1} B_m = G_m \left( s \right)
$$

**When the projector vanishes, the thing the agent is flying is not an approximation of the model. It is the model.** The host's own dynamics matrix has been cancelled out of the closed loop entirely and what remains contains only the model's. **If the host could not reproduce the target vehicle's dynamics exactly, the agent would be flying something other than the aeroplane it was trained on**, and a result obtained that way would say less than it appeared to.

**And that equality holds only inside the band the previous sections bounded.** It assumes the actuators keep up, which the rate limits deny above a few radians per second at large amplitude, and it assumes no delay, which the floor denies at every frequency. **The equivalence is exact in the algebra and approximate in the aeroplane**, and the size of the approximation is what this article has spent its arithmetic measuring.

**This is the clearest answer the article has to why the aeroplane received an X number in 2021 and not in 1992.** The machine did not change. **The thing being deceived did.** For twenty-nine years it fooled pilots, which is a task with a well-developed literature and a well-understood instrument. **Since 2021 it has been fooling software**, and the question of whether a piece of software can tell that it is not flying the aeroplane it thinks it is flying does not yet have a literature at all.

## The Aeroplane Is Twenty-Nine Years Older Than Its Number

**The X-62A first flew on 1 April 1992 and was designated on 14 June 2021**, which is 10,666 days, or 29.2 years \[[General Dynamics X-62 VISTA][ref_x62_wikipedia]\] \[[DOD 4120.15-L Addendum][ref_mds_addendum]\]. By the date of this article it has been flying for 33.7 years and has carried an X number for 4.48 of them.

$$
F = \frac{T_n - T_d}{T_n - T_0}
$$

**That fraction is 13.3 percent.** Seven-eighths of this aeroplane's flying life happened before it was an X-plane, and it is still flying, so the fraction is still falling relative to what it would have been had the number come first.

**This series has now met five distinct orderings between a designation and the aeroplane it names**, and they are worth setting beside one another because the register's own chronology conceals all of them.

| Ordering | Case |
|---|---|
| The number comes first and the aeroplane follows | the [X-1][related_post_a298_bell_x1] and most of the early series |
| The number comes after the aeroplane has stopped flying | the [X-53][related_post_a350_boeing_x53] |
| The number is allocated and no aeroplane is ever built | the [X-54][related_post_a351_gulfstream_x54] |
| The number follows the first flight by months | the [X-55][related_post_a352_lockheed_martin_x55] |
| The number follows the first flight by three decades and the aeroplane is still flying | the X-62A |

**The fifth is the only one in which the designation describes a change of purpose rather than an event in the aeroplane's life.** Nothing happened to the metal in June 2021 that had not happened many times before. **What changed was the identity of the thing the machine was built to deceive**, and the register records that change in the one row of 539 that uses the word `redesignated`.
