## Epistemic State

### What Is Assumed

**The short-period frequency against which the published rate limits are located.** 4 radians per second is a representative value for a fighter and not a measurement of any aeroplane this machine simulates. **The conclusion that the symmetric tail's full-deflection corner frequency is the lowest of the four does not depend on it**, because that is a ratio of two published numbers. **The conclusion that the tail is rate limited at the short period does depend on it**, and would fail for a model whose short period sat below 2.4 radians per second.

**The frame rate of the digital implementation.** Sixty hertz is assumed and is not known. It enters only the computational share of the delay floor. **The actuator's contribution of 49.5 milliseconds is published and is a floor on its own.**

**The separation between the two lifting controls' centres of pressure.** 0.6 chords is inferred from the published overall length and mean aerodynamic chord and from where a trailing-edge flap and a horizontal tail sit on an aeroplane of this layout. **The identity that the determinant is proportional to that separation does not depend on the value.** The condition numbers in the table beside it do, and are offered as a sensitivity rather than as a measurement.

**The host and model matrices in the worked residual.** These are representative short-period pairs. **The published F-16 aerodynamic data is tabular and graphical**, so this article has not computed the aeroplane's own control effectiveness matrix and does not claim to have done so. **What the worked example demonstrates is the asymmetry between the two rows**, which follows from a tail making moment and a flap making lift and would survive any plausible choice of numbers. **The deflection figures that follow from those matrices inherit the same status**, so the finding that the flap saturates before the tail is a statement about the shape of the problem and not a measurement of this aeroplane.

**The crossover frequency of the pilot and vehicle loop.** Three and six radians per second bracket the range the crossover model reports for compensatory tracking. **The phase the delay costs is proportional to that frequency**, so the percentages of margin consumed scale directly with an assumed quantity, and they are stated as a range for that reason. **The delay itself is published.**

**That an equivalent time delay is the right summary of the host's contribution.** The article checks the approximation rather than asserting it, finding the lag and a pure delay agreeing in phase to better than a seventh of a degree at four radians per second. **Above about eight radians per second the approximation begins to matter**, and the article makes no claim there.

**That the register's engines cell and the block convention are both correct.** The resolution offered is that the aeroplane was re-engined, which two independent sources state. **The inlet, which is the part of an engine change a block number actually encodes, is not addressed by any source this article found.**

### What Is Computed

**The model-following conditions and the projector.** The condition for exact model following, the gains when it holds, the residual when it does not, the error dynamics that residual drives, the steady error those dynamics settle to, and the rank bound that turns all of it into a count of control surfaces. **These are algebra and carry no empirical content beyond the linearity of the two systems.** The weaker condition for matching an output rather than a state is algebra of the same kind, and it is included because it shows the counting bound to be sufficient rather than necessary.

**The two short periods as modes.** The natural frequency and damping of the host and the divergent root and time to double of the model, from the trace and determinant of each matrix.

**The deflections the worked simulation demands**, from the gains that solve the matching condition, together with the angle of attack at which each surface reaches its published limit and the bound the smallest singular value places on the whole gain matrix.

**The describing-function gain of a rate limiter in deep saturation**, from the triangular output such an element produces and the known fundamental of a triangular wave. **The phase is not computed and is not quoted**, for the reason the section gives.

**The phase margin a delay consumes at a given crossover**, from the crossover model's own integrator, and the frequency at which it consumes all of it.

**The leading-edge flap schedule and the actuator in series**, from the transfer functions the report prints, including the product of the schedule's pole and the actuator's time constant.

**The invariance of the median and the non-invariance of the mean** under a strictly increasing relabelling, which is the formal content of the claim that a mean rating is a category error.

**The rank deficits by axis**, from the published list of surfaces the second flight control system commands and the standard decomposition of aircraft dynamics into three dynamic states per axis.

**The worked residual**, including the row-wise fractions of 83.3 percent and 0.05 percent and their ratio of 1,677.

**The determinant identity and the condition numbers**, from geometry alone.

**Every corner frequency in the limits table**, from the deflection and rate limits published in NASA Technical Paper 1538, together with the usable fractions at the assumed short-period frequency.

**The actuator corner frequency, its phase contribution and the equivalent delay**, from the published lag.

**Every figure in the contract analysis**, summed from the transaction record rather than read from a stated total, with 17 of 18 awards agreeing to the cent with the total the registry states separately.

**Every figure about the register**, recomputed from the parsed table, including the count of rows containing the word `redesignated` and the ranking of this row's description length.

### What the Record Does Not Settle

**Why the leading-edge flap is not commanded by the second flight control system.** The article now offers three reasons, being the surface's slow actuator, its low full-deflection corner frequency, and the fact that it is already carrying a scheduled command whose lead its own actuator very nearly cancels. **No source consulted states which of the three governed, or whether the question was ever asked.**

**Whether the near-coincidence of the flap schedule's pole and the flap actuator's corner is deliberate.** They differ by 1.42 percent. **A schedule designed for an aeroplane and an actuator sized for a surface may arrive at the same corner frequency by accident**, and this article reports the coincidence and claims nothing about its cause.

**The phase a rate-limited actuator contributes.** An ideal rate limiter contributes none. A rate-limited servo contributes up to a great deal, and how much depends on the loop around the limiter. **This article has the limit and the lag and does not have the loop.**

**Whether the change in how the acronym is expanded was deliberate.** The award record uses the older form and the prime contractor uses the newer one. **That the newer form spells the acronym exactly and the older one does not is arithmetic. That anyone noticed is conjecture.**

**What inlet the aircraft carries.** See above.

**The frame rate, the computational latency and the actual model-following architecture.** The programme has published papers on all three \[[Cotting, Stephens, Cole, Barricklow and Gray, X-62 VISTA Capabilities and Architecture, AIAA SciTech 2023][ref_scitech_capabilities]\] \[[Caraway, Harris and Cotting, VISTA X-62A Model Following Algorithm Overview, AIAA SciTech 2023][ref_scitech_mfa]\] \[[Harris and Caraway, Model Following Control Allocation For The X-62A, AIAA SciTech 2023][ref_scitech_allocation]\], and **this article cites them for their existence, their authorship and their subject, which is what the registry establishes.** It does not quote their contents and does not represent their findings.

**How widely pilot ratings are averaged in practice.** The scale's definition forbids it. **Measuring how often the field does it anyway would require a reading of the literature this survey has not performed.**

**Whether the aeroplane's own actuators have been changed since 1979.** The rate limits used here are those of a production F-16 as NASA modelled it. **An aeroplane that has been modified as often as this one may well no longer match them**, and no source consulted states the current values. **Every frequency in this article's rate-limit argument inherits that uncertainty**, and the direction of the error is not known.

## The Contemporary Literature

The survey behind this article holds **8,248 records** after gating and deduplication, drawn from 3 sweeps that retrieved 31,254 records of which 28,236 were distinct. **842 of them, 10.2 percent, are report primaries**, meaning items served by the National Aeronautics and Space Administration's technical reports server or registered under the Defense Technical Information Center's prefix. 7,775 records carry a usable year, running from 1927 to 2027 with a median of 2006. **6,556 of those, 84.3 percent, predate or share the year in which the aeroplane was redesignated.**

**Every record the gate admitted is cited below.** The clusters are ordered with the specific before the general ones they are special cases of, because a matcher that returns the first match gives a broad cluster the records a narrow one was written for.

## The Source Base

### The Pool

**3 sweeps retrieved 31,254 records of which 28,236 were distinct.** The shared rejection store removed 1,718. The subject gate admitted 8,579 and refused 17,939. Deduplication by title and year removed a further 319, leaving **8,248 records, every one of which is cited** across 15 clusters. A further 130 definitions are hand-written, being 54 primary documents and encyclopaedic anchors, 14 books whose identifiers were each resolved and read back against both the title and the author claimed for them, and 62 back-references to earlier articles in this series.

By source the admitted set is 7,804 from the Crossref registry, 542 from the NASA technical reports server and 233 through the Defense Technical Information Center's registry prefix. **842 records, 10.2 percent, are report primaries.**

### The Back-References Are Rebuilt and Not Scraped

**A356 and A357 each ship 58 reference entries whose visible link text is a raw anchor slug rather than a title.** The cause was a scraper. Each article read its predecessor's rendered list to recover the labels, one article in the chain carried no such list, the fallback silently produced the anchor, and the next article read that. **A fallback that cannot fail is not a fallback.**

This article's 62 back-references are built from a roster and then checked against the files on disk. **Every `post_url` target is confirmed to name a draft that exists, whose front-matter date matches the one in the link and whose front-matter title matches the label**, and the build fails on any disagreement. An entry whose label begins with the anchor prefix is refused outright, which is the specific defect being guarded.

### The Homonyms This Article Measured, and What They Cost

**Five of this subject's words are severe collisions and all five were measured against the registry before the first sweep rather than guessed at.**

**A bare probe for `VISTA` returned ten results of which seven were Microsoft Windows Vista administration books**, together with the grammaticalisation of the Portuguese `em vista de` and two place names. **Nothing aeronautical appeared at all.** Qualified as an in-flight simulator it returns the aeroplane's own founding papers from 1984 and 1988. The word is never an anchor alone, in a query or in a gate pattern.

**`Skyborg` cannot be qualified with `autonomy`.** That probe returned Spinoza on autonomy, contractual autonomy, the autonomy of labour law, autonomy and paternalism, and autonomy in schooling. **Autonomy is a word in political philosophy long before it is a word in aviation**, and it is one of the worst qualifiers available for this subject.

**`ACE` is the programme this aeroplane flew for and it collides with an economics subfield using the same three letters.** Agent-Based Computational Economics is abbreviated ACE and has its own journals and calls for papers. **The word `agent` makes it worse rather than better**, because a surface-active agent is an agent. The programme is only ever matched by its full name.

**`Calspan` is a strong anchor and not a clean one**, because it is a whole laboratory, so a bare probe returns its shock tunnels, a Chrysler research safety vehicle and electromagnetic wave absorption alongside its variable-stability aircraft. **And `NF-16D` is an excellent anchor while `16D` alone is not**, the latter returning a Renaissance poem and a Nova Scotia map sheet.

**Two of this article's own words are internal homonyms, which is the most dangerous kind.** `Model following` shares a participle with terrain following, which is a different problem, and `simulation` means a computer program everywhere in engineering while here it means an aeroplane. **Both are handled in this article's own gate rather than in the shared store**, because neither is anybody else's subject and a store entry would damage every other article in the series.

### Three Families Were Opened and One of Them Was Split to Open It

The shared rejection store holds **141 curated patterns across 31 tagged families**. A tagged pattern is one whose subject is somebody else's subject, and an article whose subject it is may switch it off by name. **This article switched off 3**, and says so here because a filter switched off silently is indistinguishable from a filter that never existed.

**`cockpit-displays` was written by A347 against the human-factors literature of rotorcraft displays**, as contamination of an article whose subject was unmanned. This article's subject is a pilot in a cockpit being deceived about which aeroplane is being flown, and the aircraft's own documented programme work is a programmable helmet-mounted display and a virtual head-up display. **The symbology and workload literature is the subject here and not the noise.** A356 opened it for the same class of reason.

**`teaching` was deleting the curriculum this aeroplane exists to serve.** The family untagged removed `The USAF Test Pilot School flight control systems curriculum`, `Integrating UAS Flight Test Education Into the USAF Test Pilot School Curriculum` and `Simulator-Based Flight Test Engineering as a Capstone to the Dynamics and Control Curriculum`. **The aircraft is operated by a school and flown by its students**, so the pedagogical literature is on subject.

**`physiology` did not exist before this article and was created by splitting an entry rather than by widening a family.** The biomedical computational-fluid-dynamics entry earned by A348 alternated ten terms, of which exactly one, the stem `physiolog`, names the discipline that measures a pilot. Untagged it removed `Physiological assessment of pilot workload in simulated and actual flight environments`, `Pilot Workload Analysis Based upon In-Flight Physiological Measurements`, `A Physiologically Based Model of Neuromuscular System Dynamics` and a study of simulator frame rate published in a physiology journal. **Opening the `medicine` family wholesale would have readmitted thirty-eight records on artificial intelligence in clinical trials**, so the alternative was separated into its own tagged entry on the A352 precedent. Two tests hold both halves, and the medical remainder that the split releases carries no aeronautical anchor and is refused by the gate downstream.

### An Omnibus Proceedings Volume Is a List of Subjects and Not a Subject

**The store reads a record's title and its container together, which is right, because a turbomachinery journal is real evidence that a paper is turbomachinery. It stops being right when the container is a numbered proceedings volume whose name concatenates its tracks.** One conference prints each year's proceedings as `Volume 2, Aircraft Engine, Marine, Microturbines and Small Turbomachinery, Oil and Gas Applications`, which names four unrelated fields, and that string alone removed `Integrated Flight and Propulsion Operating Modes for Advanced Fighter Engines` from an article about flight control.

**This is A354's multi-modal venue defect appearing in a different family**, and the repair has the same shape. The guard fires only when the container names a numbered volume alongside aeronautics, which is the signature of an omnibus proceedings and never of a turbomachinery journal. **A measurement of how often this class occurs found 137 records in this pool dropped by the container alone with a clean title**, most of them correctly, including a paper titled `Dogfight in the clouds` published in a volume on British archaeology in the Middle East. **The container filter earns its place and needs guarding, which are not in tension.**

### Do the Conclusions Have a Literature

**19 conclusions were probed twice, once in this article's own words and once in the field's.** The gap between the two counts is the measurement, because a thin count under an article's own phrasing is a fact about the phrasing and not about the claim.

**The probe was run after the first sweep, four conclusions came back under twenty records in the field's own vocabulary, and a second sweep was aimed at three of them.** The fourth is a claim about documents rather than about aeroplanes and no sweep will help it. The column headed `before` is the first sweep's count and the column headed `after` is the present one, so the effect of the later sweeps is data rather than assertion. **10 of the 19 conclusions gained more than half again as much coverage.**

**The equation-density review then added seven conclusions and a third sweep followed**, which is this corpus's oldest and most reliable rule. An equation pass promotes subjects, and the harvest that preceded the draft could not know which derivations would come to exist, so the subjects a later pass promotes are systematically under-represented in the pool it drew on. **Five measured under seventy records after the pass had placed equations in them**, being describing functions, pilot rating scales as a measurement instrument, direct lift control, high-lift device scheduling and the characterisation of a divergent mode.

**The rating-scale sweep was aimed at the aeronautical slice and not at measurement theory.** The general psychometric literature carries no aeronautical anchor and the gate refuses it, correctly. What this article needs is the literature on pilot rating scales themselves, which is aeronautical, which the gate admits, and which is the part that bears on the claim.

**1 of the 19 remains thin under the field's words and it is reported rather than repaired by softening the sentence.** It is the claim that the contract record and the designation register are independent and here they agree. **That has no aeronautical literature at all, because it is a claim about records**, and it rests on the two records themselves, both of which are cited and both of which a reader can check.

### What Was Read Rather Than Retrieved

**The contract analysis is computed from 79 raw transactions rather than from any stated total.** Each award's visible transactions are summed and compared with the amount the registry states separately, and 17 of the 18 agree to the cent. The remaining one is excluded because part of it falls past this article's date.

**The dateline horizon is enforced at the source and not in the prose.** 6 transactions carry an action date after 2025-12-07, of which 4 carry money totalling 782,854.00 dollars. **One of them is the only place in the entire record where the designation appears**, so an article that had filtered in the sentence rather than in the data would have reported the opposite of this record's most interesting property.

**Every published constant in the arithmetic comes from one NASA report that was downloaded and read.** Its Table 1 gives the mass, inertias and wing geometry and its Appendix A gives the actuator lag, the rate limit and the deflection limit of every surface. **The report never names the aeroplane in its title** and states in its appendix on aerodynamic data that the data came from wind-tunnel tests of subscale models of the F-16.

**The programme's own technical papers are cited for their existence, their authorship and their subject.** Those are the facts the Crossref registry establishes and they are verified there, which is a stronger check than an HTTP response. **Their contents are not quoted and their findings are not represented**, because this article has not read them.

## Conclusion

**The X-62A is the only aeroplane in this series whose designation records a change in what it was lying to.**

For twenty-nine years it lied to pilots. It was an NF-16D, a status prefix that says the modifications can never be undone, and it made a Block 30 F-16D behave like an F-22 that had not flown yet, or like an Indian fighter being designed on another continent, or like an aeroplane with flying qualities bad enough to be dangerous and a safety pilot in the back seat to make that survivable. **In June 2021 it became an X-plane, and the thing it lies to now is software.**

**The mathematics of the lie is exact and it is older than the aeroplane.** One linear system can be made to reproduce another if and only if a projector built from the host's control effectiveness matrix annihilates the demanded change of dynamics. **When it does, the gains are immediate and the imitation is perfect. When it does not, the residual is computable, it is driven by the model's own state, and no feedback gain removes it.** The condition is about how many independent directions the host's controls can reach, and it turns the design of an in-flight simulator into a counting problem.

**The count comes out at three per axis and the aeroplane has three per axis.** A symmetric horizontal tail, a symmetric trailing-edge flap and a throttle in pitch. A differential tail, an aileron and a rudder in roll and yaw. **The throttle is in the list because the speed equation is one of the three and no surface can change axial force independently**, which is the clearest illustration this article found of the argument removing the vehicle. **The engine appears in the mathematics as a column and not as propulsion.**

**And the same argument says what a simulator built round one pitch control could and could not do.** It could retune pitch stiffness and pitch damping almost exactly. **It could not change the lift curve at all**, and the ratio between those two failures, in a representative case, is 1,677. A variable-stability aeroplane without a direct lift control can imitate a different tail and cannot imitate a different wing. **The error it would leave does not decay**, because the residual is driven by the model's own state and contains no gain to tune.

**Solving the same example for its deflections rather than its residual reverses an intuition.** The tail is the powerful surface and the flap is the afterthought, and the counting bound says only that the flap must be present. **The flap is what runs out.** It reaches its published limit at 8.17 degrees of angle of attack where the tail would not reach its own until 30.5, so **the envelope of aeroplanes this machine can imitate is set by its weakest control and not by its strongest.**

**The limits that bind in practice are published and have been since 1979.** The symmetric horizontal tail, which has the most travel of any surface the second system commands, reaches its stops only below 2.4 radians per second, which is below a fighter's own short period. **The differential tail, with a fifth of the travel and the same rate limit, has 4.65 times the bandwidth.** The rate limits were set for a fighter twenty years before the simulator existed and the simulator inherited them unevenly, with the worst of it falling on the axis that does most of the work.

**The deepest limit is one-sided and no software will move it.** A model-following system drives the host's surfaces, so every delay in the host lies between the pilot and the simulated response, and the simulation can only add. **The machine can make any aeroplane sluggish and cannot make any aeroplane crisp.** The floor is at least 49.5 milliseconds from the published actuator lag alone.

**And the instrument contains the nonlinearity it was built to study.** Rate limiting is the mechanism of one class of pilot-induced oscillation, and the second flight control system drives the same surfaces through the same rate limits. **Above the published corners the host is contributing a nonlinearity of its own**, and the student cannot tell it from the model's. A rate limiter in deep saturation returns a triangular wave whose fundamental falls as the reciprocal of both amplitude and frequency, **so the harder the pilot works the less of the aeroplane comes back**, which is the positive feedback the phenomenon runs on.

**The delay floor can be priced in the currency the pilot actually spends.** A trained operator adapts until the open loop is an integrator at crossover, which leaves ninety degrees of margin, and a transport delay takes from that linearly. **At three radians per second the host consumes 14.23 percent of it and at six it consumes 28.46 percent**, before the simulated aeroplane has contributed anything at all.

**And a surface the simulation might have wanted turns out to be spoken for.** The leading-edge flap is a direct lift device and would be a fourth column in the longitudinal matrix, and the second system does not command it. The published schedule that does command it asks for a lead of two above 3.625 radians per second, **and the flap actuator's own corner sits 1.42 percent from the schedule's pole**, so across the band where the simulation lives the surface delivers a gain rise of 0.8 where the schedule asks for 1.8. **The lead is not merely reduced. Its sign is reversed.**

**The answer then comes back on a scale with ten boxes and no metric.** The Cooper-Harper rating is ordinal by construction, its only claims about magnitude are the two level boundaries, and a statistic is meaningful on such a scale exactly when it survives every strictly increasing relabelling of the boxes. **The median does and the mean does not**, so a mean of such ratings asserts something the scale declines to supply. **The instrument is far more precise than its own readout.**

**The money says what all of this costs and never once says what the aeroplane is called.** 73 transactions and 29,085,924.37 dollars over 11.6 years, 81.2 percent of it to the laboratory that owns the simulation system and 18.8 percent to the prime contractor that owns the airframe and the autonomy interface. **The obligation rate steps by a factor of 3.17 at the redesignation** and the first payment lands 31 days after it. **And in 73 transactions the string X-62A appears 0 times.**

**That absence is the article's opening finding and it deserves to be its closing one, because it is not a clerical curiosity.** A designation is a claim about a vehicle's purpose, made by one part of a government to another. **The part that buys the fuel and the spares had no use for the claim**, because for its purposes the aeroplane had not changed and the contract line was the same contract line. **Both records are right. They are answering different questions.**

**The register's own sentence, which is not official wording and which the compiler marks as reconstructed, turns out to be corroborated by the accounting system anyway.** Three months after the redesignation the Air Force obligated 799,956.00 dollars under a line that names the Skyborg programme by name. **The two records are maintained for unrelated purposes and they agree**, which is the strongest thing this series has been able to say about a reconstructed description since the register stopped being a primary source one article ago.

**What the next article inherits is a register that has now been unofficial for two designations running**, and the X-63A, allocated ten months after this one, is the third.
